title: Jeremiah 31:38–40
context: The LORD promises that the city will be rebuilt “to the LORD,” and he traces its boundaries: from the tower of Hananel to the gate of the corner (31:38), the measuring line going on to the hill Gareb and turning toward Goah (31:39), and the whole valley of the dead bodies and of the ashes, with the fields to the brook Kidron and the corner of the horse gate toward the east, all holy to the LORD and never again plucked up or thrown down (31:40). The tower of Hananel and the horse gate appear in Nehemiah 3:1, 3:28, and 12:39, the corner gate in 2 Kings 14:13 and 2 Chronicles 26:9, and the tower and corner gate together in Zechariah 14:10. Gareb and Goah are otherwise unknown, and their locations are uncertain. Many readers connect the valley of the dead bodies and ashes with the Valley of Hinnom, where Jeremiah announced judgment (compare 7:31–32; 19:6), though that identification is not certain. Readers take the promise in several ways: some see its first fulfillment in the rebuilding under Nehemiah; many see it pointing beyond that to the holy city of God’s people in Christ (compare Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2); others expect a future rebuilt Jerusalem. These views run across both traditions rather than dividing them, and the notes present them without choosing.

verses.text: “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that the city will be built to the LORD from the tower of Hananel to the gate of the corner.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD promises that “the city will be built to the LORD from the tower of Hananel to the gate of the corner.” Arminian readers see a promise of restored community dedicated to God, with named landmarks anchoring hope in a real place. Readers in this tradition differ over whether the main fulfillment is the return, the church, or a future Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the city built “to the LORD” as his own work and possession, and many read the promise as pointing beyond the rebuilt walls of Nehemiah’s day (compare Nehemiah 3:1) to the people of God in Christ. Shared ground: both traditions read the landmarks as real places in Jerusalem, and both hold the eschatological application with care.

verses.text: The measuring line will go out further straight onward to the hill Gareb, and will turn toward Goah.
verses.arminianNotes: “The measuring line will go out further straight onward to the hill Gareb, and will turn toward Goah.” Arminian readers see the measuring line as a sign of planned, generous restoration, perhaps extending beyond the city’s former bounds. Gareb and Goah are otherwise unknown, so their locations remain uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the measuring line as an image of the LORD’s ownership and ordered purpose for his city (compare Zechariah 2:1–5; Ezekiel 40:3). Shared ground: both traditions hold the identification of Gareb and Goah loosely, and both read the measuring as a pledge that the city’s restoration is real and secured by God’s design.

verses.text: The whole valley of the dead bodies and of the ashes, and all the fields to the brook Kidron, to the corner of the horse gate toward the east, will be holy to the LORD. It will not be plucked up or thrown down any more forever.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The whole valley of the dead bodies and of the ashes … will be holy to the LORD. It will not be plucked up or thrown down any more forever.” Arminian readers see a striking reversal: a place many link with the Valley of Hinnom and its judgment (compare 7:31–32) becomes holy, showing God’s power to redeem even defiled ground.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same reversal as God’s sovereign grace sanctifying what was unclean, and the promise “not … any more forever” as the end of the cycle of judgment announced in 1:10 and 31:28. Shared ground: both traditions hold the Hinnom identification with some caution, and both read the verse as a pledge of lasting holiness, however its fulfillment is understood.
